NEW YORK, Nov 13 : An internet trade group sued New York on Friday, seeking to block a state law requiring social media platforms that contain potentially addictive features to provide state-approved warning labels for users. In a complaint filed in federal court, NetChoice said the law violates the free speech protections of the US Constitution's First Amendment by compelling its members to convey the state's "preferred message" about online safety. The office of New York Attorney General Letitia James, who enforces the state's laws, declined immediate comment. NetChoice has more than 30 members including Alphabet's Google and YouTube, Facebook and Instagram parent Meta Platforms, Snapchat parent Snap and ByteDance's TikTok. It has filed many lawsuits challenging regulation of social media businesses.

Signed by Governor Kathy Hochul last December, the New York law requires social media platforms with infinite scrolling, auto-play and algorithmic feeds to warn about potential harm to younger users. It requires the display of a "warning" from the US Surgeon General that while social media may benefit some young users, "excessive use may be associated with significant mental health harms." The statement is modeled after findings in 2023 by former US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy. NetChoice said New York's law is "designed to block, burden, and browbeat social media users" by subjecting them to the warning when they sign on and after multiple hours of use, with no way to bypass it. "Unlike a static warning on a product label, these warnings repeatedly interrupt users and block access to protected speech," NetChoice said. NetChoice filed a similar lawsuit against California last month. It also said New York's law is similar to a Colorado law that a federal judge blocked in November 2025, citing the First Amendment. Colorado is appealing that decision. New York's law is scheduled to take effect on January 1.

Source: Reuters

Nov 13 : Institutional-investor interest in Anthropic’s initial public offering is outpacing the early days of SpaceX's roadshow, according to two people familiar with the companies’ offerings. The Anthropic roadshow is scheduled to run through next Wednesday, when the AI company is expected to price the $64 billion deal. Anthropic and its investment banks are meeting prospective investors in New York, Boston and San Francisco to gauge demand for the offering, one of the people and a third person familiar with the matter said.  The IPO drew about two times the orders for the shares available by the end of Tuesday, the first day of the roadshow, one of the people said. By the end of Thursday, the book was six times oversubscribed, one other person said. SpaceX’s IPO was two times oversubscribed by the end of its second day of roadshow, Reuters previously reported. While that single-digit subscription rate would be considered modest for many highly anticipated IPOs, bankers and investors said demand is impressive for the Anthropic offering given the size of the IPO. They expect Anthropic's order book to grow substantially as the roadshow progresses, reflecting strong early demand, two of the people said.

Details of the IPO, including the demand for shares, could change, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Anthropic declined to comment. During the roadshow, investors are grappling with two fundamental questions as they assess the offering and the company's valuation: whether Anthropic can maintain its lead as competitors such as Alphabet’s Google rapidly catch up in developing advanced AI models, and whether its Claude chatbot can maintain its lead beyond coding, in the broader market for knowledge workers. TIME OF UNCERTAINTY IN AI The questions underscore the challenge of valuing a company whose revenue is growing fast but whose long-term competitive position remains uncertain. Investors are trying to determine whether the AI industry will ultimately be dominated by one or two players or support several leading companies, and whether Anthropic can sustain premium pricing if rivals offer comparable models. Meanwhile, investors are also weighing the limitations of the information Anthropic is providing during its IPO roadshow. One investor who attended a roadshow meeting said the company had not provided detailed answers to some of the questions raised. Anthropic declined to comment on the investor's remarks. While companies are not always able to address every investor question during roadshows, some investors remain cautious about an offering at a high valuation amid a broader shakeout in the AI sector, with the limited disclosure leaving some questions unanswered. One of the group meetings during the roadshow also did not include a conference call allowing institutional investors to dial in and ask questions, according to an investor who attended that meeting — a departure from standard roadshow practice. Representatives from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley largely read from prepared remarks rather than solicit  questions at that meeting, the person added. Morgan Stanley declined to comment. Goldman Sachs did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REVENUE AT CENTER OF VALUATION DEBATE Investors are arriving at widely different estimates of how quickly Anthropic's revenue will grow, creating a broad range of potential valuation outcomes. The key figure underpinning valuation models is Anthropic's projected 2028 revenue, which banks estimate at around $270 billion to $280 billion and use to apply enterprise-value-to-revenue multiples and arrive at their valuation estimates, two of the people familiar with the projections said. For a high-growth company like Anthropic, investors typically give significant weight to future revenue growth when assessing its value. Some sell-side projections put Anthropic's revenue at around $52 billion to $53 billion in 2026, rising to $135 billion to $137 billion in  2027, one of the people said. Certain buy-side projections are running 10 per cent to 15 per cent higher for 2026 and 2027, an investor who has placed an order in the IPO said. But buy-side forecasts also vary significantly. One investor who conducted due diligence on the IPO but decided not to participate has a more conservative outlook that is about 30 per cent below the sell-side estimate for 2028. Differences between sell-side and buy-side forecasts are common. Sell-side analysts' estimates tend to track a company's own projections more closely, while investors may build in more optimistic or conservative assumptions about future growth. Companies, in turn, have an incentive to set conservative targets ahead of an IPO, leaving room to beat estimates and raise expectations after listing. The comparable companies used in the valuation models also reflect the difficulty of finding direct peers for Anthropic. SpaceX and cybersecurity company CrowdStrike are among the names being used as benchmarks, one of the people familiar with the projections said. The focus on Anthropic's projected 2028 revenue contrasts with SpaceX, whose valuation case relied on projected 2029 revenue that some investors viewed as particularly aggressive. Anthropic's valuation debate, by comparison, is anchored in a forecast for a year closer to its expected public listing.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK: “He’s irreplaceable,” Larry Ellison said. The year was 2009 and Oracle’s then-chief executive officer was talking about his friend Steve Jobs, who had recently returned to lead Apple after a liver transplant. Pundits would later go on to say the same about Jeff Bezos, that Amazon.com’s founder and CEO had “no viable successor”. (Both companies, of course, would go on to do just fine without their founders.) It’s worth remembering those prophecies as that word - irreplaceable - gets bandied around with abandon about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down Thursday (Nov 12) after nearly a week of turmoil at the company he cofounded and the industry he anchored.  One of many examples: “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire posted on X, a sentiment Elon Musk endorsed.

Revelations from the New York Times on Wednesday, that Huang had an extramarital relationship with the company’s vice president of healthcare, made it impossible for the board to let him keep his job. While less shocking than Huang’s earlier admission that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, he had clearly violated the company’s code of conduct to “avoid situations where our actions create a conflict”. Before board members could make the case that Huang was the victim of a honeypot scheme. But there’s no convenient explanation for a relationship with a subordinate.

CAN NVIDIA SURVIVE WITHOUT JENSEN HUANG? The board named CFO Collette Kress as the interim CEO, but now its members will have to plan for a future without Huang at the helm. This appears to be something they had rarely considered before, after allowing Huang to structure the company almost entirely around himself. The question now is whether he had also built it to survive without him. As Harvard Business School professor Rakesh Khurana put it to me: “The difference between a cult and a religion is that one outlasts the other.” At Nvidia, the evidence suggests that Huang created a system much more akin to the former.  The company has no chairman, no number two and no public succession plan. Huang had 60 direct reports whose job it was to quickly carry out his decisions, Bloomberg News has reported. Few other executives had a broad purview or responsibilities and instead focused on narrow products or technologies. Other executives had some public exposure but were always overshadowed by Huang, who delivered hours-long keynotes at events.  On earnings calls, as the Wall Street Journal noted, Huang fielded questions from analysts mostly by himself, leaving scripted comments to others - a regular practice at Nvidia but atypical at other companies. His board lacked the expected heavy hitters for a company of its size and import; other than Huang, it has no sitting CEOs.

Related:

Commentary: Everything Jensen Huang said about China is out the window

Commentary: Jensen Huang is bigger than Nvidia – and it’s a problem

A REAL FAILURE OF LEADERSHIP? None of that necessarily means Huang can’t be replaced. There was no finding another Jobs or Bezos either - they were both singular leaders. But what they did, which appears to be missing at Nvidia, was methodically build companies designed to carry on their doctrines without them. Both created internal structures that institutionalised their ways of operating and thinking that allowed their successors to thrive: Apple’s stock returned nearly 2,800 per cent during Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure as CEO that ended in September; Andy Jassy has overseen a roughly 50 per cent increase since he took over at Amazon in 2021. At Apple, Jobs was a micromanager who was involved in every detail of the company. But he also taught employees to anticipate how he would solve problems. “The organization has been thoroughly trained to think like Steve,” Fortune reported in 2009. “People could envision, ‘This is what Steve would do.'”  He also had a clear number two in Cook, a manufacturing and supply chain guru, who had a trial run as CEO when Jobs was out on medical leave. Jobs made sure it wasn’t always the Steve Jobs show either. Cook and other executives were given public exposure by appearing alongside him on stage and on earnings calls. (It’s worth noting that Cook is being floated as a possible replacement for Huang, including by President Trump.) At Amazon, Bezos turned his management philosophy into an actionable way of operating - a set of leadership principles that Jassy and other executives helped him write. Bezos picked Jassy as his first shadow, a role in which he followed around the CEO for about 18 months. That’s when the two came up with the idea for Amazon Web Services, and then Bezos gave Jassy a wide berth to run it. By the time Jassy was tapped as CEO, he had already run a hugely important and valuable business. Part of the genius of both Bezos and Jobs was that they figured out how to turn their personal capabilities into corporate culture and competencies.  The parallels are hard to find at Nvidia, which is a real failure of leadership by Huang. His successor will have to figure out how to run a company built around someone who is no longer there. That should be one part of Huang’s legacy that no one tries to replicate.

WASHINGTON, Nov 13 : Risks tied to the artificial intelligence sector surged to become the top-cited concern for financial stability, according to a semi-annual report released by the Federal Reserve on Friday. The US central bank's Financial Stability Report found potential risks from the technology itself and the breakneck investment in the sector as the preeminent concern of survey respondents. Eighty-seven percent of contacts surveyed cited AI as a salient risk to the financial system, as respondents pointed to worries about cyberattacks, risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing, and the possibility of an AI earnings slowdown spurring a broad market correction. Just 50 per cent of those surveyed cited AI as a risk in the May version of the Fed's survey. Other top concerns cited in the survey also had heavy AI implications. The second most-cited concern was regarding a broad correction in risk assets at 52 per cent of those surveyed, and cyberattacks specifically were flagged as a worry by 43 per cent of respondents. Forty-eight percent of those surveyed also fretted about higher long-term interest rates, while 43 per cent cited fiscal debt sustainability as a worry. The survey was conducted in September and October, meaning respondents weighed in before the latest turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, where CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving Chinese businesswoman whom the New York Times has reported is under suspicion as a Chinese spy. The survey also preceded the results of recent midterm elections in which the American public's rising concerns about AI were also a central issue.

The increased focus on AI was underpinned by the report itself, as the Fed devoted a chunk of the report to examining the rapid increase in debt issuance tied to data centers and other advanced computing infrastructure. The Fed report found that advanced computing-related debt issuance had surged to $680 billion by October 2026, already a fivefold increase on debt issued in all of 2023. Advanced computing-related borrowing now accounts for nearly a third of all nonfinancial investment-grade corporate debt issuance, after amounting to less than 6 per cent three years ago. The Fed noted in its report that the rapid influx of debt issuance and investment in AI-related infrastructure could be compared to the broadband telecom investment cycle of the late 1990s, although the Fed said it is possible the current investment cycle may soon surpass that era. And the central bank focused on the complex financing arrangements underpinning some of this investment, noting that arrangements like long-term contracts, leases and guarantees allow hyperscalers and other large firms to support financing such projects by smaller third parties, and graphics card designers and hyperscalers often further contribute to investments via equity. Data collected by the Fed found that debt, guarantees, and not-yet-commenced leases on this infrastructure could exceed $3 trillion. The Fed said such "circular financing" dynamics could allow the largest firms to absorb losses in the event of a downturn, minimizing the impact on the broader financial system. However, it could also mean that those firms' exposure to such a downturn could be "substantially larger" than indicated by their on-balance-sheet liabilities. "The complex interlinkages among firms engaged in the data center buildout, public credit markets, private lenders, and special purpose financing vehicles create vulnerabilities that necessitate close monitoring," the report stated. Elsewhere in the financial system, the Fed found that asset valuations across a range of classes remained high, due in part to investor enthusiasm about AI. The report noted that investment in the AI sector has been a significant driver of US economic growth this year, and an unexpected downturn in corporate earnings could prompt a market decline, tighter credit, and reduced investment, which would all weigh on the economy. Such a downturn could also be exacerbated by relatively high levels of leverage in some portions of the financial sector. The Fed noted in its level that leverage among hedge funds, particularly the largest firms, remains at the highest levels recorded since they began gathering such data in 2013.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 13 : Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang turned to law firm Paul Weiss amid his rapid fall this week, tapping a firm that reached a controversial deal with President Donald Trump last year and whose own longtime leader was forced to step down in February. Huang resigned on Thursday after more than 30 years leading the top AI chipmaker, following reports that he had extramarital affairs with three women, including an Nvidia executive and Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy. Paul Weiss, Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang had no immediate comment on Friday about the nature of the law firm's work for Huang. New-York based Paul Weiss, with more than 1,500 lawyers, long has been a go-to for corporate boards and executives facing regulatory scrutiny, misconduct allegations or other reputational crises.

It built a reputation pairing lucrative work for Citigroup and other business clients with liberal advocacy and fundraising for Democratic candidates, including Kamala Harris. But the firm drew sharp criticism within the legal profession and from Democrats last year after striking a deal with Trump to rescind an executive order the Republican president issued against it in March 2025. Trump's order suspended security clearances for the firm's lawyers and restricted their access to government buildings and officials, citing its internal diversity policies and its association with a prosecutor who investigated the president. Paul Weiss pledged in its settlement to dedicate $40 million in pro bono legal services to support "mutually agreed" projects with the White House, sparking similar deals by eight other law firms. Its longtime chairman Brad Karp defended the accord, calling Trump's order an existential threat.  The tumult facing Karp ramped up early this year, after emails surfaced showing Karp's extensive personal and business communications with the late convicted sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein. Karp resigned from his leadership post in February, saying the reports about Epstein had created a distraction that was not in the firm's interests. He has not been accused of wrongdoing. GO-TO FIRM FOR CORPORATE CRISES Paul Weiss has a stable of former senior Justice Department officials and others who frequently step in for clients when crisis strikes. BlackRock in 2021 hired partner Loretta Lynch, who was US Attorney General under President Barack Obama, to assist with an internal probe of former employees' claims of sexual harassment and discrimination. Huang is working with Paul Weiss partners Melinda Haag and Walter Brown, the New York Times reported on Thursday. Haag served as US attorney in San Francisco during the Obama administration. She and Brown did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not independently confirm which lawyers at the firm are representing Huang. The Republican leaders of several US House committees, including Foreign Affairs, addressed a letter to Brown on Thursday stating they wish to interview Huang in closed-door session next month. Haag successfully defended former Fitbit executive Katherine Mogal, who was acquitted in 2020 of federal charges alleging theft of trade secrets from a rival wearable-device maker. Brown is on the team defending Meta Platforms in a lawsuit by an Australian mining magnate over scam ads on Facebook showing him promoting fake cryptocurrency. Nvidia’s board has hired another top firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Kratz to conduct an independent investigation. That probe will be led by Wachtell’s Joon Kim, a former senior federal prosecutor in Manhattan.

Nov 13 : Jensen Huang as a Bollywood matinee idol, as a character from "The Matrix" or donning a red velvet suit on a poster for an alternate-universe version of "The Spy Who Shagged Me": the Nvidia co-founder's extramarital affairs, including with a Chinese businesswoman, set the Internet afire this week. The storm of AI generated video and images, many of the clips were likely made with the help of Nvidia graphics chips, provided some light relief to a scandal that toppled one of the tech industry's most prominent CEOs, wiping out hundreds of billions of investor value and triggering investigations worldwide. The Huang memes competed for the spotlight with a raft of comedic takes on the more than 12-hour outage of Microsoft services including Outlook and Teams, topping off a week that kicked off with the latest Stephen Miller vampire memes after U.S. President Donald Trump named him as chief of staff, effective Monday. But it was humor on the crisis surrounding Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia that dominated many social media feeds, with many of the clips likely made using Nvidia graphics chips, RaviKunvariyaX quipped on X.

Nov 13 : Nvidia's board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll. Haas' name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang's exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He is among several candidates being considered and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia's finance chief Colette Kress is the interim CEO.

Nov 13 : Shares of AI-related US companies dropped again on Friday, with neoclouds among the worst hit, fueled by fresh jitters over AI financing following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt exit. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 declined 2 per cent, on pace to erase about $800 billion in market value if the losses hold through the close. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index also shed 5.1 per cent, facing a more than $560 billion wipeout for the day. CoreWeave and Nebius Group, neocloud firms backed by Nvidia, slumped 8.8 per cent and 9 per cent, respectively, extending their sharp declines from Thursday when longtime CEO Huang stepped down after revelations of extramarital affairs. Nvidia, under Huang, has financed infrastructure built around its chips, a strategy that has driven demand but also raised questions about circular funding flows between the chipmaker and its customers.

"It's a short-term death blow to the industry because the amount of vendor financing and financing guarantees that Nvidia and Jensen Huang stepped into are now over," said Thomas Hayes, chairman of Great Hill Capital LLC. Further, Nscale, a British cloud provider also backed by Nvidia, amended its IPO filing to say it expects to report a net loss of $1.7 billion in the nine months ended September 30, wider than the $433.3 million net loss a year ago. A media report on Friday said Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Huang. Arm shares were last down 4.8 per cent. Chip stocks, widely regarded as among the biggest winners of the AI boom, also dropped. Advanced Micro Devices fell 10.7 per cent and Broadcom lost 5.9 per cent after both gained for the last five sessions. Memory chipmaker Micron Technology shed 5 per cent while data storage companies Western Digital and Sandisk dipped 6.6 per cent and 8.1 per cent, respectively. Photonic product makers Lumentum and Coherent, along with AI server makers Dell and HPE, fell between 5.3 per cent and 9 per cent each. Utilities and equipment suppliers exposed to the AI boom, including GE Vernova, Constellation Energy and Vistra, eased about 2.2 per cent to 3.5 per cent each. AI hyperscalers were also mostly lower, barring Meta Platforms, which rose 1.2 per cent. Oracle, Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft fell between 0.2 per cent and 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's quarterly earnings and AI lab Anthropic's much-awaited public markets debut are set for next week and could prove to be catalysts for sentiment towards AI. "You have no idea what to expect from Nvidia. That's the problem. This company is pure uncertainty right now," said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers.

The notice, dated November 10, said the provider told Uber on October 9 that the credentials had been compromised and used to access Uber's account with the provider. TechCrunch reported on Friday that the provider was Fireworks AI and that the data included drivers' license information.

Sweden-based Asmodee publishes and distributes many globally known board games such as Catan, Ticket to Ride and Carcassonne. It also distributes trading card games from other publishers, including Pokémon, Hasbro's Magic: The Gathering and Bandai Namco's One Piece trading card games.

"What's clear is that our industry benefits from very strong sociological dynamics of spending time with your loved ones," Koegler said in an interview on Friday. He expects game nights to remain a popular Saturday plan, especially over Christmas, when darker weather makes games more appealing. The end-of-year holidays are a key sales season for game and toy companies. Board games have gained popularity among 16- to 25-year-olds, who are now putting them "at the heart" of their social life, Koegler said. An international barometer compiled by Asmodee and Kantar in 2026 showed that 74 per cent of the so-called "Gen Z" thought that in-person experiences were more important than digital ones. Koegler also pointed to rising attendance at trade events such as Spiel Essen and Gen Con, and hobby stores engaging local player communities, as two indicators that Asmodee's efforts to engage players through in-person events were working. "We see increasing of sales (in hobby stores), which means an increase in sell-out from them, because they are this nexus of local communities," Koegler said. ORGANIZED PLAY SUPPORTS TRADING CARD GAMES Organized play also holds a strong place in the success of trading card games, a category that Koegler has previously described as extremely strong and lasting. "All the events are packed because people really engage," he said. The Netherlands' largest board game event Spellenspektakel, which also hosts Europe's biggest trading card game event CardCon, reported 33,000 visitors at its 2026 edition on November 7-8, with a sold-out first day. Asmodee's sales grew 18.4 per cent in the board game category and 51.6 per cent in trading card games during its most recent quarter that ended in September. Hasbro's earnings were also boosted by its flagship trading card game Magic: The Gathering ahead of the holiday season.

BERLIN, Nov 13 : Germany's information security office BSI warned on Friday of ongoing vulnerabilities in some of Danish firm Danfoss' industrial cooling appliances, following cyberattacks on refrigeration systems across Europe. The systems in question should be taken offline when possible or otherwise any connection should be secured via VPN, or Virtual Private Network, BSI said in a security advisory on its website. SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 13 : Federal Reserve officials expect artificial intelligence will reshape the US economy, an idea that proponents of the technology in Silicon Valley have plastered on billboards and TV and pushed in public debate as they channel trillions of dollars into data centers and billions into their bank accounts. But how the region's new tech boom evolves, and on what timetable, remains a wild card for central bankers responsible for managing inflation and employment in the short term. In a public forum on Monday in San Francisco, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will try to understand better the risks and benefits he and his colleagues may have to balance — from the possible large-scale loss of jobs to the promise of rapid economic growth and falling prices. The forum, the only scheduled public event of the five task forces Warsh established early in his tenure this year to review issues of major importance to the Fed, will take him to the epicenter of an emerging industry he sees as a "hinge point in history," even as last week's midterm elections sparked a backlash against rapid data center construction and raised the specter of deepening inequality. For all of AI's disinflationary potential, Warsh is convening the discussion while the frenetic AI buildout is having the opposite effect — driving up prices in a way that increasingly concerns many Fed officials, with no clarity for when it may let up and with the possibility the central bank may need to slow the very thing Warsh sees as revolutionary.

More broadly, what seemed a clear proposition of supercharged growth and buoyant productivity when Warsh spoke while auditioning for the Fed job — he was also an investor in AI firms but sold his holdings under Fed ethics rules — is now at the center of a national debate that could change the industry's trajectory. Though driven by local politics, the concerns range from local land use to the impact on children's and societal mental health, the potential for stress in financial markets as capital is channeled through increasingly complex AI funding vehicles, and, most recently, risks to national security after revelations about a top tech industry executive's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. "We have to make sure that AI is used responsibly and ethically," Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee said recently as she joined a movement to ban local data center construction that has taken root just across San Francisco Bay. "It can't become a tool that compounds the biases that are already built into our systems. It can't be a tool for harm, for discrimination, or for displacement." EVOLVING VIEWS It may be difficult for participants in the three-hour forum on Monday to cover the sweeping set of issues that will determine whether AI deployment accelerates or slows, and therefore how deep an impact it might have on inflation, employment and other data the Fed watches. An agenda published by the San Francisco Fed says the event, including three panels of speakers bookended by comments from Warsh, will offer "input from a wide range of stakeholders on technology's implications for the economy and the labor market." It will be a homecoming of sorts for the Fed chief. He attended nearby Stanford University with some of the tech industry's leading figures and appointed one of them, Marc Andreessen, to chair the task force that will focus on AI, which Warsh has come to call "super intelligence" in line with President Donald Trump's wishes. Other members of the productivity and jobs task force include Chad Jones, a Stanford University economics professor now working with the internal think tank of AI firm Anthropic, which is on the verge of an initial public offering that would value the company at more than $1 trillion, and Asha Sharma, who runs Microsoft's Xbox business. Fed officials began focusing on AI even before Warsh took the helm, with the pace of research and discussion accelerating after the release of the ChatGPT generative AI chatbot in 2022 and the start of breathtaking changes for a technology that a decade ago had trouble telling a cat from a kitchen table. Thanks to breakthroughs in large language models and the massive assemblage of computing power, AI is now solving advanced math and medical problems, turning novice entrepreneurs into software engineers, and offering bespoke "agentic" services that can do legal or scientific research or take over personal bill-paying and daily planning. While Warsh initially saw AI as providing a downdraft on inflation through higher productivity — a free ride of sorts that could allow central bankers to keep interest rates lower than would otherwise be expected — he has taken a more nuanced view since arriving at the Fed in May. The shift reflects the uncertain timetable for productivity benefits, the potentially inflationary investment needed to realize them, and views about job-market impacts that range from a lift-all-boats boost to a Dickensian world of chronic underemployment. 'TRULY HISTORIC' INVESTMENT At a forum in Oakland in September, where the city's mayor issued her warning about AI, Fed Governor Lisa Cook, whose academic research focused on innovation, reiterated concerns that AI would lead to "at least a temporary increase in the unemployment rate" and possibly a jump in the underlying level of joblessness. Fed Governor Michael Barr raised similar concerns on Thursday, saying the US should prepare for "serious short-term disruptions" to the job market depending on how fast AI is deployed and whether it remains broadly available and affordable to businesses regardless of size. For the moment, though, AI investments are propping up US growth, stock-market gains, and consumer and business spending that might otherwise be unremarkable. "You have this investment that is truly historic. You are talking railroad-plus-interstate-highways-historic," Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said recently at a chamber of commerce event in South Carolina where attendees pumped him for insight on what the AI boom might mean. "If that historic investment does not pay off and people scale back, you worry what is going to happen." Although all the members of the task force Warsh picked are from the tech world, neither they nor the Fed chief will have the last word on how any recommendations find their way into Fed policy. That matter will be left to officials like Barkin, who said he hoped the discussion on Monday would cover the full landscape of issues. "I'm hopeful we'll hear the strongest possible evangelist's view, as well as the strongest possible other view," Barkin said. "Then we'll have a chance to wrestle with it."

STARBASE, Texas, Nov 13 : SpaceX launched the 15th flight of its Starship spacecraft from Texas on Friday on a mission the company hopes will be the first round-trip rocket voyage to orbit and back to the very spot where it left Earth, a key test of Elon Musk's effort to build a fully reusable rocket system. Plans call for Starship's uncrewed upper-stage vessel to re-enter the atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit and return to its launch tower on Saturday for an engine-controlled touchdown assisted by the giant mechanical arms of a pioneering catch-landing mechanism. SpaceX had intended to use the same return-flight and "chopstick"-arm technology to recover Starship's lower-stage booster rocket shortly after the two parts of the spacecraft separated within minutes of the launch. But the Super Heavy booster, for reasons not immediately clear, was diverted from its return flight path to a fixed point over the Gulf of Mexico and momentarily hovered in the air before exploding a short distance over the sea surface.

The vehicle reached orbit about 27 minutes after launch, SpaceX said. KEY TEST OF REUSABILITY Bringing the top portion of the spacecraft intact back to the platform where it was launched would mark a breakthrough in the ambitions of Musk, who founded SpaceX in 2002, to reduce spaceflight costs by developing a fully recyclable rocket system. The combined vehicle, consisting of the main Starship cargo-and-crew vessel perched atop its Super Heavy booster rocket and standing 40 stories high, roared off its launch pad from SpaceX's South Texas Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville. The flight marked Starship's 15th test flight since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites to orbit. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavor for SpaceX's satellite-connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a rocket ship still under development. Starship 15 began releasing its cargo of 26 satellites about 36 minutes into its flight in a payload-delivery operation expected to take less than an hour to complete, the company said in a livestream presentation of the mission. Musk's space and AI business views Starship as key to expanding its network of Starlink internet satellites and, in the future, deploying a swarm of orbital AI data-processing centers dubbed Starmind, as the company positions itself to become a high-tech infrastructure provider. SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and a payload of satellites to orbit for the first time despite some rocket engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an upper stage splashing down intact into the Pacific Ocean before bursting into flames. RETURN-FLIGHT AND RECOVERY PLANS For Friday's mission, the company was aiming for both the lower-stage Super Heavy and the upper-stage Starship to return to the spacecraft's Texas launch site for safe landing and recovery. Plans called for the orbital cruise vessel to touch down about 22 hours after launch. SpaceX has said it would be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" if that feat is achieved. SpaceX has previously returned the 236-foot (72-meter) Super Heavy booster three times to its launch pad after sending Starship to space, with the booster flying itself back to Earth minutes after launch and gently descending upright into the grasp of a pair of large mechanical arms fixed to the launch tower. The last such "tower catch" was in March 2025. It was not immediately clear why Friday's attempt failed. Starship was expected to descend from space after completing 14 orbits around Earth, setting up its debut catch landing for Saturday afternoon. Musk has said he expects to achieve a pace of weekly Starship launches by the first half of 2027. NASA has helped fund Starship's development with roughly $3.2 billion since selecting the rocket ship in 2021 to serve as a lunar lander for its astronauts under the multibillion-dollar Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion of its own funds into the rocket's development. NASA and SpaceX expect Starship to land humans on the moon by 2028, though several major testing objectives remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back. Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship tanker rockets in orbit, a critical process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA's Orion capsule, in Earth's orbit next year for Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA's planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 13 : Amazon  has a secret plan to ensure shoppers never need to leave its site: own the world’s product information.   Called World Product Graph, the initiative seeks to hoover up data on virtually every item for sale on Earth, whether Amazon stocks it or not, according to an internal document reviewed by Reuters, and to people familiar with the matter. In so doing, Amazon could truly become the everything store, offering deep data on a vast array of goods and cutting in to Google's dominance in online search, while also fending off rival Walmart's growing e-commerce business. It also serves to address the continued rise of AI agents, software that can complete shopping tasks autonomously for users. According to the document, Amazon's own AI-driven search agent was providing inaccurate information.

And if fully implemented, World Product Graph could draw shoppers away from rival e-commerce sites that have far less data.  “Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites,” according to the document. “These answers exist, but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums.” Reuters could not determine if or when this plan may be implemented, though the document, written like a press release, has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027. "Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn't necessarily reflect our current plans," said Amazon, in a statement. "We're constantly working on new ideas and technologies to make Amazon's product catalog comprehensive, accurate, and helpful for customers." Already, many consumers begin researching products on Amazon. But according to a 2025 Morgan Stanley research report, the 16 per cent of online shoppers who do so on Amazon is dwarfed by Google’s 57 per cent. However, when customers know exactly what product they plan to buy, Amazon has the advantage, with 41 per cent of searches starting there, compared with 23 per cent for Google and 18 per cent for Walmart. 'THE EVERYTHING STORE' World Product Graph “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” the document says. That will entail some brands and retailers contributing product data continuously to Amazon, but also Amazon independently crawling other retailers’ websites.   Reuters could not determine how Amazon planned to crawl the sites or whether it would need to seek permission in all cases. Amazon has already signed up Coca-Cola and Bayer, among others, to contribute product data, the document says. And the company held a “CEO-level P&G/Amazon summit” for a trial with Procter & Gamble. The companies didn't respond to requests for comment. Amazon is shuffling staff internally to get the project off the ground, according to one of the people, though Reuters could not determine if the October 1 date is a realistic deadline for making the plan public.  The document laying out the plan is what is known internally as a PR/FAQ — press release and frequently asked questions — which is typically a six-page narrative memo laying out the rationale and business case for a new product or service. Not all PR/FAQs lead to a service being introduced and, the people said, World Product Graph could be modified or aborted due to financial or other concerns.  The initiative is part of Amazon’s Selection & Catalog Systems unit, according to the document, and is being organized under Robert Tekiela, a vice president in the division. He did not respond to a request for comment. With the more complete data, Amazon can help users determine with more certainty which is the most recent model or colorway of a vacuum cleaner or tablet computer while also guiding them toward more subjective criteria like which is best for them based on their shopping history or other data, the document shows. The project would also tackle what it said had been problems with Amazon’s AI-powered search engine known as Rufus — which the company began calling “Alexa for Shopping” in May. “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete, but customers lack expertise to detect these errors,” the document states. Further, users conduct about 83 million searches weekly using Rufus, and running them is “expensive,” according to the document. More data would allow Amazon to use less expensive models, more efficiently. “I used to spend an hour on Reddit figuring this stuff out,” says a fake customer in an imagined quote in the document. “It’s like the store finally knows what it’s selling.”  In its statement to Reuters, Amazon, referring to the PR/FAQ, said "the usage figures are significantly outdated" and that its data shows that Alexa for Shopping is roughly 97 per cent accurate globally. BATTLING AGENTS World Product Graph would help serve at least one other important function — staving off the growing threat of alternative AI shopping agents, the people said. CEO Andy Jassy sought during the company's third-quarter earnings call to downplay agents' impact, saying “few customers are doing much shopping this way yet” and that Amazon’s advertising business has been minimally impacted.    Yet Amazon executives have grown wary of AI shopping agents that may send customer traffic to other sites that have greater or more complete data, according to people familiar with the matter. Meta’s Muse agent, for instance, has proven popular with customers already, garnering more than 10 million users in the US and Canada since launching in September. Amazon in the same month blocked Muse from its retail site and last year sued AI firm Perplexity to prevent similar access, a case that is ongoing.   Jassy said Alexa for Shopping has been used by over 400 million people in the past year. Muse, however, "has the potential to become the most widely used consumer AI application since ChatGPT,” JPMorgan said in a research note. Responding to a post saying xAI's Grok agent was blocked on Amazon, Elon Musk wrote on X last month: “Maybe we should start a competitor to Amazon."    By creating the world's most extensive storehouse of product data, Amazon could ensure AI agents working on behalf of shoppers will be compelled to seek products out on Amazon.com and not other retailers’ sites, the people said. That would also help protect Amazon’s growing advertising business. Shares of the Seattle retailer were down just over 1 per cent at $264.12 at midday on Friday, part of a broader selloff following the resignation this week of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.  Employees have described World Product Graph as the beginnings of an effort to make the site a one-stop shop for buying anything imaginable, an expansion of existing services known as “Buy for Me” and “Shop Direct,” which list on Amazon products sold on other sites, allowing customers to buy them with Amazon as an intermediary. “Customers have always been able to find products on Amazon,” Tekiela said in the document. “What’s been missing is understanding – how do these products relate to each other, which one is right for me, and what else should I consider?”
